---
title: "Analysis of survival and characteristics of mutations"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
editor: visual
---

The aim of this analysis is to explore the survival rate of patients and how the characteristics of the mutations (variants, length, location with respect to chromosomes) may affect survival.

#### Loading libraries and the data

```{r}
#| message: false
library("patchwork")
library("here")
library("tidyverse")
library("broom")
library("gt")
```

```{r}
load(here("data", "03_cancer_augment.RData"))
```

## Analysis of survival based on cancer type

First, the percentage of survival for all cancer types is compared between men and women.

To give an overview of the different cancer types, below is a boxplot of the survival for each type.

```{r}
g1 <- ggplot(data = clinical_augment,
            mapping = aes(y = cancer_type,
                          x = os_months)) + 
  geom_boxplot()+
  labs(title = 'Survival for each cancer type',
       x = 'Time (Months)',
       y = 'Cancer type')
g1
```

Here, we have constructed a col-plot of the survival chance for all cancer types, grouped by sex.

```{r}
clinical_augment |> 
  group_by(sex) |> 
  summarise(number_of_patients = n(),
            alive = sum(status == 'LIVING', na.rm = TRUE),
            survival_percent = alive / number_of_patients * 100) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = sex,
                       y = survival_percent,
                       fill = sex)) + 
  geom_col(position = 'dodge')+
  labs (title = 'Survival percentage for all cancer types',
        x = 'Sex',
        y = 'Survival percent (%)')+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
    angle = 20,
    hjust = 0.75))

```

There is little to no notable difference between the survival of men or women when looking at all cancer types.

We have now done the same col-plot but for each cancer type. This shows that the cancer with the lowest survival rate is glioma, followed by breast cancer.\
The highest chance of survival is for Skin-cancer, non-melanoma (This is only for 1 patient who survived, so is not a good, representative sample size).\
Disregarding the odd one, the type with the collectively highest survival percentage is melanoma.

```{r}
#| message: false
clinical_augment |> 
  group_by(cancer_type, sex) |> 
  summarise(number_of_patients = n(),
  average_survival = mean(os_months, na.rm = TRUE),
  alive = sum(status == 'LIVING', na.rm = TRUE),
  survival_percent = alive / number_of_patients * 100) |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = cancer_type,
                       y = survival_percent,
                       fill = sex)) + 
  geom_col(position = 'dodge')+
  labs (title = 'Survival percentage for each cancer type',
        x = 'Cancer type',
        y = 'Survival percent (%)')+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
    angle = 20,
    hjust = 0.75))

```

The different survival rate for each cancer type, also depends on the gender of the patient.\
This show that glioma has the lowest, and that melanoma has one of the highest survival rate.

Skin cancer, Non-melanoma has a survival rate of 100%, because there is only data from one patient, making it misleading.

```{r}
survival_curve_test <- clinical_augment |> 
  group_by(cancer_type,os_months) |> 
  summarise(
    deaths = sum(status == 'DECEASED'),
    living = sum(status == 'LIVING'),
    .groups = 'drop'
  ) |> 
  
  arrange(cancer_type,os_months) |> 
  
  group_by(cancer_type) |> 
  mutate(
    at_risk = rev(cumsum(rev(deaths + living))),
    survival = cumprod(1 - deaths/at_risk)
  ) |> 
  ungroup()


#survival_curve_test
g1 <- ggplot(data = survival_curve_test,
             
             mapping = aes(x = os_months,
                           y = survival,
                           color = cancer_type))+
  geom_step()+
  labs(title = 'Overall survival by cancer type',
       x = 'Overall survival (months)',
       y = 'Survival probability',
       color = 'Cancer types')+
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = 'bottom')+
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(
      title.position ='top'))
g1
```

This is a survival probability curve over time for each cancer type. This curve shows that the survival of the patient heavily depends on the individual types of cancer. To highlight some of the types with the greatest differences, below is the same curve, where only two cancer types are shown.

```{r}


#survival_curve_test
g1 <- ggplot(data = survival_curve_test |> 
             filter(cancer_type %in% c('Melanoma','Glioma')),
             mapping = aes(x = os_months,
                           y = survival,
                           color = cancer_type))+
  geom_step()+
  labs(title = 'Overall survival by cancer type',
       x = 'Overall survival (months)',
       y = 'Survival probability',
       color = 'Cancer types')+
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = 'bottom')
g1
```

To look more closely on two quite different cancer types, in terms of survivability, we have shown glioma with one of the lowest survival percentages, and melanoma with one of the highest survival percentages.

Here it is more clear, that the type of cancer impacts survival quite a lot.

In the rest of this analysis, the focus is put on survival of patients who died during the study, as survival for living patients represents their last recorded follow-up appointment.

```{r}
clinical_mutation |> 
  filter(status == "DECEASED") |>
  mutate(cancer_type = fct_reorder(cancer_type, os_months)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = os_months,
             y = cancer_type))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  labs(x = "Survival (months)",
       y = "",
       title = "Overal survival of deseased patients for various cancer types")+
  theme_minimal()
```

This plot shows the general survival of patients with different types of cancer. Highest median number of months is for renal cell carcinoma, though there is quite a large variation. Colorectal and breast cancer are at the bottom and show less variation in the number of months survived.

```{r}
clinical_mutation |> 
  filter(status == "DECEASED") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = variant_type,
             y = os_months))+
  geom_boxplot()+
  theme_minimal()+
  labs(x = "Type of mutation",
       y = "Survival (months)",
       title = "Survival of patients affected with different mutation types")
```

ONP (oligonucleotide polymorphism), which affect more than 3 consecutive nucleotides are the mutations with the highest median length of survival, while INS and DEL have a lower median length of survival.

### Analysis of correlation between average length of mutation and survival

```{r}
#| message: false
patient_mutation_summary <- clinical_mutation |> 
                              select(patient_id, length_mutation, status, total_mutations, os_months, cancer_type)|> 
                              filter(status == "DECEASED") |> 
                              group_by(patient_id, os_months, total_mutations, cancer_type) |> 
                              summarize(mean_length_mutation = mean(length_mutation),
                                        max_length_mutation = max(length_mutation))
```

Fitting a linear model for each cancer type, relating the number of months survived to the length of the mutation.

```{r}
patient_mutation_estimate <-  patient_mutation_summary |> 
                              group_by(cancer_type) |> 
                              nest() |> 
                              ungroup() |> 
                              mutate(model_object = map(.x= data,
                                                        .f = ~lm(formula = os_months ~ mean_length_mutation,
                                                                 data = .x)),
                                     model_object_tidy = map(.x = model_object,
                                                             .f = ~tidy(.x, 
                                                                        conf.int = TRUE,
                                                                        conf.level = 0.95))) |> 
                                     unnest(model_object_tidy) |> 
                                     filter(!term == "(Intercept)") |> 
                                     select(c(cancer_type, p.value, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)) |> 
                                     ungroup() |> 
                                     mutate(q.value = p.adjust(p.value, 
                                                               method = "BH"),
                                            is_significant = ifelse(q.value < 0.05, 
                                                                    "yes", 
                                                                    "no"))
saveRDS(patient_mutation_estimate, here("data", "summary_lm.rds"))
```

```{r}
patient_mutation_estimate |> 
  gt(rowname_col = "cancer_type") |> 
  tab_header(title = md("Statistical summaries of linear regression"))
```

According to the statistical summaries computed here, only Renal Cell Carcinoma shows a correlation between the number of month the patients survived and the length of the mutation in number of nucleotides. This is due to the significantly low p-value.

```{r}
clinical_augment |> 
  group_by(status) |> 
  filter(cancer_type == "Renal Cell Carcinoma") |> 
  distinct(patient_id) |> 
  count()
```

There are 143 (54 + 89) patients who were diagnosed with Renal Cell Carcinoma, 54 of whom are included in the linear model fitting above.

```{r}
#| message: false
patient_mutation_summary |> 
    filter(cancer_type == "Renal Cell Carcinoma") |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = mean_length_mutation,
               y = os_months))+
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5)+
    geom_smooth(method = "lm")+
    labs(x = "Average length of mutation",
         y = "Survival (months)",
         title = "Survival as a function of average mutation length in patients with Renal Cell Carcinoma")+
    theme_minimal()+
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12))
```

From this plot, we can see that the correlation is not very pronounced. What can be observed is that mutations are generally SNPs (length of 1) and that surprisingly, longer mutations are seemingly correlated to longer survival.
